title: The Science of Mechanics Instruction that Sticks
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. uses a colleague's grammar warm-up series, Mechanics Instruction that Sticks, as a case study in what a curriculum resource can and cannot do. He begins with Hattie's finding that teacher credibility (trust, competence, dynamism, immediacy) is among the strongest influences on achievement and argues that no purchased resource can substitute for it. He then maps the warm-ups onto Make It Stick: a coherent base of foundational knowledge, spaced retrieval practice, and interleaved, varied practice rather than massed drills. He pushes back on the fashion of teaching mechanics only in the moment of need, arguing that language knowledge belongs in a guaranteed and viable curriculum, kept short so it does not crowd out the lesson. The piece closes with testimonials and a purchase link, so it is part pitch, but the learning-science reasoning carries real argument.
points: Teacher credibility, which Hattie breaks into trust, competence, dynamism and immediacy, is built over a career and cannot be bought, so any resource works only in credible hands.
Short daily warm-ups can apply retrieval practice and interleaving, which explains why students taught this way retained mechanics knowledge better.
Stuart rejects teaching grammar only when needed and argues mechanics should be a planned, sequenced part of the curriculum.
Efficiency matters: five to ten minutes at the start of class avoids the fatigue of long lessons for students who already have the concept.
quotes: Basically, if students don’t perceive you as a person who can make a difference in their lives — if they don’t believe in you (see Figure 1) — then they, in Hattie’s words, “just turn off.” [1]

These four components, according to Hattie, combine to become teacher credibility. This, of course, isn’t something you can buy; you develop it over the course of a career through consistent, focused effort.

Too often, I think we English teachers fall into the trap of approaching grammar and mechanics knowledge with hesitancy. The wisdom of the day suggests that it’s best to teach kids the mechanics knowledge they need only right when they need it, delivering mechanics instruction solely within one-on-one or small group settings.

It is important, of course, not to allow mechanics instruction to stretch from 5-10 minutes at the start of class to 30-40 minute lessons. This, indeed, would become tiresome for students who’ve largely “got it” and need to move on.
Periodic practice arrests forgetting, strengthens retrieval routes, and is essential for hanging onto the knowledge you want to gain.
Second, as already mentioned, Doug’s warm-ups are intentionally concise — this isn’t “massed practice.
You won’t make a bunch of photocopies of the first unit of warm-ups, hand them out, and then magically see students write more mechanically sound sentences.
